aiDisclosure: I use AI as a research and engineering instrument. I define the questions, scope, and evaluation criteria; orchestrate the workflows; review intermediate and final outputs; and make the final technical and editorial decisions. Each artifact states its verification level and the division of human and AI work.
focusLine: Returning to education in a PhD program, or a research team at a company, in human-centered AI for learning, scientific reasoning and discovery. I work on it at Bucket Foundation, where Research OS is a tool for exploration and mastery.
heroCopy: Mathematician, data scientist, AI-systems builder, and educator. I build research tools, production software, and AI-assisted knowledge systems, from a 12.2M-row map of the research economy to open machine-learning tools that a lab can run on a laptop.
researchStatement: I am returning to education in a PhD program to master my own knowledge interactions with the data I meet in my research. My question: how should AI be designed and built into human learning, knowledge work and scientific discovery so that gains in machine capability produce gains in human capability? I treat human capability and human-AI capability as priors, predictors of both the rate of scientific discovery and a society's exposure to existential risk. I work on it at Bucket Foundation, where Research OS is a tool for exploration and mastery: an educational knowledge graph and research environment that routes learners from questions through prerequisites and evidence to new knowledge. The work on this site is the foundation: research infrastructure at 12.2M rows, working papers, open machine-learning and quantum tools benchmarked against published baselines, and production AI systems that keep a human in the loop.

researchInterests.title: Human-centered AI for learning and scientific discovery
researchInterests.body: How AI should be designed and built into learning, knowledge work, and scientific reasoning so that machine capability grows human capability: adaptive assistance that models a person's goals and knowledge state, controlled human-AI experiments that measure delayed transfer, independent problem solving, calibration, and reliance, verification of AI-assisted work, and what degrades once a person stops checking. Research OS for K‑12 at Bucket Foundation is the sandbox.

researchInterests.title: AI systems for research knowledge
researchInterests.body: Retrieval and generation grounded in primary sources: hybrid BM25 and dense retrieval over full-text papers, answers that carry their citations, and a 12.2M-row provenance-tracked graph of the research-funding economy underneath.

researchInterests.title: Machine learning for scientific discovery
researchInterests.body: Models that make a scientific measurement cheaper or a hypothesis testable: protein stability prediction, Markov state models of molecular dynamics, ADMET property prediction, and quality control for cryo-EM and electrophysiology. Benchmarked against published baselines, CPU-only, open source.

researchInterests.title: Learning methods for quantum computing
researchInterests.body: Neural decoders for quantum error correction inside a real-time budget, learned search over quantum-optimization circuits, and how to partition a workload across CPU, GPU, and QPU.

researchInterestsNote: These are active study questions rather than completed results. Each one links to code, a benchmark, or a working paper where one exists.

studies.title: Research Atlas
studies.role: Creator and human research lead. AI-assisted.
studies.question: Can the global research-funding economy, grants, funders, organizations, people, and the outputs they produce, be reconstructed as one normalized, provenance-tracked graph, open enough for anyone to audit or extend?
studies.method: A connector-based pipeline maps eight funder sources (NIH, NSF, UKRI/GtR, CORDIS, Gates Foundation, Wellcome Trust, Sloan Foundation, DFG) and OpenAlex research-output records into one canonical schema. Entity reconciliation runs on ROR (organizations), ORCID (people), DOI (works), and Crossref Funder IDs. Ingestion is idempotent and resumable, with cached raw pages, partitioned parquet shards, provenance on every row, and edge-level validation tests across a six-entity graph model (Funder to Grant to Organization, with Person and Work linkages).
studies.scale: ~1.67M grants · ~192.7K organizations · ~1.44M people · 75 funders · ~$1.04T normalized funding · ~12.2M graph rows
studies.humanContribution: Defined the schema, chose the reconciliation strategy and identifier systems, directed the connector architecture, and reviewed validation results.
studies.aiContribution: AI-assisted implementation of individual connectors, transformers, and test scaffolding under that direction.
studies.verification: Edge-level validation tests run in CI against the reconciled graph. Full independent replication of every connector has not been separately audited by a third party.
studies.limitations: Funding amounts are normalized across currencies and years with standard assumptions that can shift totals at the margin. Coverage is limited to the eight funders and OpenAlex; it is not a census of global research funding.

studies.title: The structure of public research funding
studies.fullTitle: The structure of public research funding, 2015-2025: concentration, cross-funder co-funding, and the funding-to-output relationship in a reconciled NIH/NSF/EC/UKRI grant graph
studies.author: Gianangelo Dichio, with the research-atlas working group, Bucket Foundation
studies.question: How concentrated is public research funding across institutions, what fraction of funded work is co-funded across multiple funders, and how does funding translate into measurable output across agencies?
studies.method: Built on 887,016 reconciled grants from NIH, NSF, EC, and UKRI (2015-2025). Computes institutional concentration (Gini coefficient), cross-funder co-funding rates, and funding-to-output ratios by agency.
studies.scale: 887,016 grants · Gini coefficient 0.929 institutional concentration · ~25% of funded works co-funded across multiple funders
studies.humanContribution: Framed the research questions, directed the analysis, and wrote the paper.
studies.aiContribution: AI-assisted drafting and computation under direct review.
studies.verification: Preprint, version 1.0. Peer review has not yet occurred.
studies.limitations: Funding-to-output rate differences reflect agency research missions as much as efficiency; the paper does not claim a causal ranking of funder effectiveness.

studies.title: The Knowledge-Access Gradient
studies.question: Every prior technology widened access to consuming knowledge, to read, learn, and reach what others discovered. None widened access to producing it. Can AI become the first scalable channel that helps people cross that boundary?
studies.method: Maps knowledge access across a six-level depth ladder (L0 basic literacy through L5 producing new knowledge) using a corpus of 78,326 observations across 219 countries and 30 indicators, benchmarked against UN SDG 4.
studies.keyFindings: World-average access falls from 82.5% at basic literacy to 0.14% at the research frontier, roughly a 270x decline. The rich-poor gap is under 2x at literacy and roughly 75x at the frontier. About 99.86% of humanity only consumes knowledge; roughly 0.14% ever reaches where it is produced.
studies.humanContribution: Framed the question, defined the depth ladder and indicator set, directed the synthesis, and wrote the paper.
studies.aiContribution: AI-assisted data synthesis and drafting under direct review.
studies.verification: Working paper, version 1.1. Not yet peer reviewed.
studies.limitations: Indicator coverage varies by country, and the depth ladder is a constructed framework rather than a standardized international metric.
studies.personalNote: This is the clearest statement of why I do this work: Bucket Foundation, early research-methods writing, education reform, and the current interest in AI-assisted scientific discovery are all downstream of this question.

studies.title: Neural Decoders for Quantum Error Correction
studies.role: I chose the questions and experiments, reviewed the code and outputs, and am studying the repository.
studies.question: Can learned decoders match minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) on quantum error correction codes while staying inside a real-time decoding budget?
studies.method: Benchmarks a ladder of neural decoder families (MLP, CNN, GRU, ConvGRU, 3D-lattice convolution, GNN) against MWPM on the repetition and rotated surface codes, using Stim for circuit simulation, PyMatching for the MWPM baseline, and PyTorch for the learned decoders. Includes a comparison against reported results on public Google Sycamore syndrome data.
studies.humanContribution: Chose the research questions and experiment design, directed the benchmarking methodology, and reviewed the code and results.
studies.aiContribution: AI generated substantial implementation work: the decoder architectures, training loops, and much of the benchmarking code.
studies.verification: Independent reproduction of the repository's headline claims is in progress. The repository's own hardening pass found that an initially favorable real-time surface-code claim did not survive testing under circuit-level noise and single-shot timing, and the repository documents that correction rather than hiding it.
studies.limitations: This is not peer-reviewed research and is not evidence of quantum advantage. It is a benchmarking study comparing classical and learned decoding strategies.

studies.title: Quantum Similarity and Kernel Estimation
studies.role: I chose the questions and experiments, reviewed the code and outputs, and am studying the repository.
studies.question: Can swap-test and Hadamard-test overlap estimation reproduce classical cosine similarity and kernel computations on real quantum hardware, and where does the classical cost of state preparation eliminate any advantage?
studies.method: Implements swap-test and Hadamard-test overlap estimation for cosine similarity and quantum kernels over amplitude-encoded states, checked against classical ground truth on a noiseless simulator, with a small six-pair demonstration on IBM Quantum's ibm_fez processor.
studies.humanContribution: Chose the research questions and experiment design, directed the benchmarking methodology, and reviewed the code and results.
studies.aiContribution: AI generated substantial implementation work: the estimator circuits, kernel assembly, and mitigation code.
studies.verification: Hardware observations (the ibm_fez demonstration) are kept explicitly separate from modeled-noise mitigation experiments in the repository. Independent reproduction is in progress.
studies.limitations: Not peer-reviewed research and not evidence of quantum advantage. The repository states directly that arbitrary amplitude-state preparation costs up to O(2^n) gates, which removes any demonstrated end-to-end speedup for similarity search.

work.title: Nucleus Brain

work.method: AI orchestrator routing work across specialist sub-agents over MCP (Model Context Protocol): tool-calling workflows, a rubric-based evaluation loop scoring agent output on defined criteria, and human-in-the-loop review at each stage.
